Why JSON has backslashes: escaping and double encoding

Backslashes can be necessary JSON syntax, real characters in a value, or evidence that a document was serialized into a string. Inspect the value and its expected type before changing it.

By ParseCove · Published 27 November 2026

On this pageFour statesInspect a layerDecode deliberatelyKeep real dataFix the producerFAQ

Separate the value from its representation

An object in memory is not the same thing as JSON source text. Serializing the object produces a document. Serializing that document as a string adds another layer: its quote and backslash characters must be escaped to fit inside a JSON string. A debugger may also display a string with escapes without changing the stored value.

StateComplete exampleWhat to inspect
JSON object document{"id":"001"}Parsing returns an object
JSON string containing that document"{\"id\":\"001\"}"Parsing returns a string, whose contents are JSON text
Ordinary string value"001"The leading zeroes are data, not a reason to parse again
Debugger or log representationA quoted display of a stringCheck raw text and the runtime type; do not count visible slashes alone

The first two examples can describe related information while having different top-level types. A formatter may correctly leave the second as a string: formatting is not permission to rewrite the application’s data model. A document may also contain just one field holding JSON text, while its other strings should stay untouched.

Inspect one encoding layer

Choose a known example and inspect one parse. The inspector never recursively rewrites string fields or guesses which values should change type.

{"id":"001","ready":true}

After one parse: string. One top-level string layer was decoded.

One parse gives JSON text held in a string. Only parse that text again if your data contract expects an object.

Decode one known layer, then check the result

The sample below deliberately serializes an object twice. The first parse returns a string; the second returns the known original object. This is a demonstration of a controlled input, not a general instruction to keep parsing arbitrary values until they stop looking like JSON.

JavaScript: a deliberately double-encoded sample

const record = { id: "001", ready: true };
// This example deliberately serializes an object twice.
const body = JSON.stringify(JSON.stringify(record));
const first = JSON.parse(body);
console.log(typeof first); // string

// A second parse is deliberate here: we know this sample holds an object.
const second = JSON.parse(first);
console.log(typeof second); // object
console.log(second.id); // 001

Python: the same known layers

import json

record = {"id": "001", "ready": True}
body = json.dumps(json.dumps(record))
first = json.loads(body)
print(type(first).__name__)  # str

# Decode again only because this known sample is a serialized object.
second = json.loads(first)
print(type(second).__name__)  # dict
print(second["id"])  # 001

For a production response, check the producer’s contract first. If the field is documented as an object, fix duplicate serialization upstream where possible. If it is explicitly documented as JSON text, decode that identified field when needed. Do not automatically parse every string in a tree: even a string containing valid object syntax may be a template, an example, a signed body or ordinary text.

Decode an identified payload field

const envelope = {
  payload: '{"id":"001"}',
  note: '{"keep":"this is ordinary text"}'
};
// The producer's contract identifies payload as JSON text.
const payload = JSON.parse(envelope.payload);
console.log(payload.id); // 001
console.log(typeof envelope.note); // string

The JSON unescape tool handles one string layer at a time. Choose Complete string when the outer double quotes are present, or String content when the copied fragment omits them. Its result is text; it does not silently traverse an object and change the types of nested fields.

Why deleting backslashes can corrupt the data

JSON uses escapes to represent quotes, reverse solidus characters and control characters inside strings. A path containing real backslashes needs an escaped source representation. A newline in the value is represented by a backslash-n sequence in JSON source; an actual unescaped line feed between the source string’s quotes is invalid.

A valid document with real path characters and a newline

{"path":"C:\\temp\\report.txt","message":"Line 1\nLine 2"}

After parsing, the path contains its actual separators and the message contains a newline. Removing every backslash from the source changes those values or breaks the document. Likewise, replacing every escaped quote can turn a quote inside a value into an accidental end-of-string character. A valid escape is not evidence of a problem.

Preserve exact identifiers as strings. Values such as "001", "true" and "null" can intentionally be text. Numeric IDs beyond a parser’s exact range need special care before any number conversion. The data tools on this site reject unsafe integer literals; this inspector uses the same strict JSON checks.

References: RFC 8259, especially strings and interoperability and MDN: JSON.parse.

Fix the extra serialization at its source

Trace where an object becomes text. A common extra layer appears when application code serializes a value and then hands the resulting string to a response helper that serializes again. Structured logs and message envelopes may intentionally store a JSON document inside a string field. The right fix depends on that contract, not on the number of visible backslashes.

  1. Inspect the raw response or log field and record its expected type.
  2. Parse one known JSON document and check whether the returned value is an object, array or string.
  3. If a documented string field holds another JSON document, decode that field deliberately for the consuming task.
  4. When you control both ends, pass the intended value type through the boundary and serialize at the agreed layer.
  5. Compare representative values before changing the producer or rewriting stored data.

Do not rewrite signed payloads, templates or raw audit records merely to make their representation easier to read. Decode a copy for inspection and retain the original where its exact bytes matter. JSON escaping is also different from UTF-8 byte misdecoding, HTML entity encoding and URL encoding; this guide’s examples address JSON serialization layers, not every problem called “double encoding”.

When JSON text is stored inside one CSV cell, use the CSV nested-value example to distinguish a string cell from columns or rows expanded out of an object. For configuration syntax and types, see YAML vs JSON.

Once you have a JSON document, use JSON minify and format to change its layout, or compare JSON values to inspect differences between two versions. Formatting a document and decoding a string are separate operations.

Common questions

Does a backslash always mean double encoding?

No. It may be required JSON syntax, an actual character in a string, or a display convention. Inspect the source and resulting value type. A path with escaped separators can be correct.

Should I call JSON.parse twice?

Only when you know that the first parsed value is a string containing the next JSON document expected by your contract. The sample here is deliberately constructed that way. Do not apply a fixed number of parses to unrelated responses.

Can I remove all escape characters?

There is no general operation that removes every escape while preserving every value. Parse the supported syntax at the correct layer. If the source is damaged, recover the intended original instead of deleting characters until it parses.

Why does one field remain a string after parsing?

That is the type represented by the document. The field might intentionally contain JSON text, an identifier or an example. Decode only the identified field when the producer and consumer agree on that meaning.
